title: Are Fortresses, and Many Other Things to Which Princes Often Resort, Advantageous or Hurtful?
coreMove: Judge security devices by circumstance: whether they create dependence, expose weakness, or fail against popular hatred.
sourcePressure: The chapter reviews arming or disarming subjects, fostering factions, cultivating enemies, winning former opponents, and building or demolishing fortresses. No device receives a universal answer. Arming subjects can bind them in a new principality; disarming new provinces may be necessary. Factions prove weak in war. Former enemies can become useful if they need the prince. Fortresses help only in some circumstances, and no fortress saves a hated ruler.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version asks whether fortresses are good or bad. The writer must preserve the conditional logic across security instruments and end on the strongest test: the best fortress is not being hated by the people.

hook: trust people versus control people debate
fortress as generic emotional wall metaphor
counterintuition: most people assume fortresses protect you, but actually people matter
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and list your defenses

exampleSpecs.domain: a new mountain prince deciding whether to arm villagers who helped him take the pass
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler afraid that armed subjects will become dangerous later
exampleSpecs.stakes: disarming them immediately signals distrust and forces him toward hired guards, while selected arms can make former suspicion into dependence
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: He pauses over the disarmament basket, then hands pass-guard spear rings to the villages that carried his banner up the ridge.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Pass-guard spear rings sit beside an empty disarmament basket.

exampleSpecs.domain: an old kingdom annexing a rebel province and deciding which local fighters must be softened over time
exampleSpecs.audience: a governor adding a province to an existing state rather than founding a new one
exampleSpecs.stakes: the adherents who opened the gate need reward, but the broader province cannot remain an armed body separate from the old state's soldiers
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the review, he ties green service cords on the gate-openers and sends the rest of the province pikes to ceremonial storehouses far from the border.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Green service cords lie beside bundled province pikes.

exampleSpecs.domain: a tributary glass city where rulers have nursed two guild factions until a foreign army approaches
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince who believed division kept the city manageable in peace
exampleSpecs.stakes: when war arrives, the weaker faction opens a side gate to the invader and the stronger faction cannot resist alone
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The prince predicts the rival guilds will balance each other, then the smaller guild lifts its colored glass token and places it on the foreign captain's side of the gate map.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Two colored glass guild tokens sit on opposite sides of a gate map.

exampleSpecs.domain: a new ruler recruiting former opponents who now need his favor to survive
exampleSpecs.audience: a prince deciding whether early enemies can serve more faithfully than secure old friends
exampleSpecs.stakes: old friends may neglect his affairs from comfort, while former opponents must cancel distrust by visible service
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: He sets the old enemy's forfeiture slip beside a new road-guard commission and watches the man sign service that his own survival now depends on.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A forfeiture slip lies beside a fresh road-guard commission.

exampleSpecs.domain: a coastal duchess choosing whether to rebuild an inner citadel after returning from exile
exampleSpecs.audience: a ruler whose people hated the old citadel as a bridle rather than a refuge
exampleSpecs.stakes: the citadel might protect her from a first attack, but rebuilding it tells the people she fears them more than foreigners
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The mason slides the citadel keystone forward, and the duchess turns it over to reveal the old tax scratches before ordering the foundation filled.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A citadel keystone with tax scratches rests on a mason's plank.

exampleSpecs.domain: a countess sheltering in a keep after her consort is killed while hostile townspeople wait for foreign help
exampleSpecs.audience: an adviser deciding whether the keep is a real solution or a temporary refuge
exampleSpecs.stakes: the keep buys time only because outside help cannot yet reach the people; if foreigners join them, stone will not overcome hatred
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The adviser marks the keep door as time gained, then draws the foreign road opening beside the angry town list and crosses out fortress as sufficient.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A keep-door tally sits beside an angry town list and a foreign road sketch.

skillTargets: distinguish when arming subjects builds dependence from when disarming an acquired province fits the old-state/new-province condition
analyze why fostered factions help only in peace and fail when outside force arrives
apply the test for winning former enemies whose survival now depends on service
evaluate fortress decisions by whether the prince fears people or foreigners and whether popular hatred makes stone useless

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one security device in a historical regime: arms distribution, faction balancing, former-enemy recruitment, or fortresses. Write the circumstance that makes it useful and the circumstance that makes it expose weakness.
